title: Measuring the ankle–brachial pressure index

brief.scenario: You are a core surgical trainee in a vascular assessment clinic. A 68-year-old with exertional left calf discomfort is attending for a resting Doppler ABPI. A training manikin and Doppler equipment are available. The patient also has type 2 diabetes.
brief.task: Explain, demonstrate the measurement sequence, calculate both indices from the supplied readings, interpret results and advise next steps. You have 9 minutes.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: an ABPI is a measured ratio interpreted alongside symptoms and Doppler signals—not a magic number.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: relying on an automated high index to rule out PAD in diabetes.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: identify, consent, rest supine and check that the clinical examination is safe.

flow: Demonstrate manual Doppler pressures in both arms and both ankles.

grid.label: Introduction, identity and consent
grid.borderline: Introduces but omits consent or discomfort warning.
grid.pass: Checks identity, explains cuffs/Doppler and obtains consent.
grid.high: Adds accessibility, pain and stop-signal agreement.

grid.label: Red flags and limb review
grid.fail: Ignores rest pain or tissue loss.
grid.pass: Asks about rest pain, wounds, sudden changes and checks feet.
grid.high: Distinguishes limb threat from routine claudication and prioritises urgent review.

grid.label: Position and equipment
grid.borderline: Positions supine but omits cuff-size check.
grid.pass: Resting supine where feasible; selects suitable cuff and manual Doppler.
grid.high: Explains positioning limitation and documents exceptions.

grid.label: Brachial pressures
grid.borderline: Attempts both but records just one.
grid.pass: Obtains systolic readings from both brachial arteries.
grid.high: States highest brachial pressure becomes common denominator.

grid.label: Ankle pressures and signals
grid.pass: Measures dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pressures in each leg and records waveform nature.
grid.high: Mentions peroneal artery where feasible and repeats uncertain signals.

grid.label: Calculation
grid.fail: Divides ankle by its own lower arm result incorrectly.
grid.pass: Uses highest ankle pressure per leg divided by highest arm pressure.
grid.high: Shows units cancel and checks plausibility of both results.

grid.label: Interpretation
grid.fail: Says normal/high ABPI excludes PAD in diabetes.
grid.borderline: Calls a low result abnormal without context.
grid.pass: Recognises low left index and potential falsely high right with diabetes.
grid.high: Correlates waveform, symptoms and need for further vascular testing.

grid.label: Management and compression safety
grid.fail: Recommends compression from single potentially unreliable value.
grid.borderline: Offers vascular review but no safety explanation.
grid.pass: Requests appropriate clinical/vascular assessment and avoids unsupervised compression decisions.
grid.high: Differentiates symptomatic PAD and suspected limb-threat escalation.

grid.label: Closure and documentation
grid.pass: Documents pressures, ratios, Doppler signals and plan; checks understanding.
grid.high: Makes a succinct bilateral report with limitations and safety-netting.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I need the machine now. Put your foot up.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Checking blood pressure in your leg.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: It hurts when I walk; should I be worried?

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The patient has diabetes. How will you position them?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Sitting is fine; I can start on one arm.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: You have readings from both arms: right 140, left 150 mmHg. Which do you use?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will just use 140 because it is nearer.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What ankle arteries will you measure?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Only the easy pulse I can feel.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Left ankle: posterior tibial 90, dorsalis pedis 96; right ankle: posterior tibial 200, dorsalis pedis 192.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I will use 96 over the 140 I chose: about 0.69, so only mildly reduced.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What does the right ankle measurement mean?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The right ratio is high, so diabetes cannot affect the artery and the right leg is definitely fine.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Yes, there is no need for further assessment.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: ABPI done. No need to write the Doppler signals.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I am the core surgical trainee. I will check blood pressures at both arms and ankles with a cuff and handheld Doppler. The cuffs squeeze briefly. Is that all right?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Yes.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Before starting: do you have pain at rest, a wound that will not heal, or any sudden worsening?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: No wounds or sudden change. My left calf aches after about 200 metres and settles with rest.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Thank you. I will inspect both feet and check pulses as well; please tell me if a cuff hurts.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: There is no ulceration. How do you position the patient?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: After allowing rest I position them supine if possible and select correctly sized cuffs and a manual Doppler.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Which pressures do you take?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Systolic pressures from both brachial arteries. I use the higher brachial pressure as the denominator for both legs.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Right arm 140; left arm 150 mmHg.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: So the denominator is 150 mmHg.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: At each ankle I use the Doppler over both dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries, recording the pressure when flow returns on cuff deflation and noting signal quality.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Left posterior tibial 90, dorsalis pedis 96; right posterior tibial 200, dorsalis pedis 192 mmHg. Left signal monophasic and right signal poorly compressible.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Left ABPI is 96 over 150: 0.64. Right ABPI is 200 over 150: 1.33.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Does that mean my right leg is healthy?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Not necessarily. Diabetes can cause stiff vessels and spuriously high or normal ABPI readings, so I do not exclude disease on the right from this value alone.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: What happens next?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The symptoms and low left ABPI warrant vascular assessment and risk-factor management. I would review Doppler waveforms and arrange further tests if needed. Compression decisions need the full assessment, not this ratio alone.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will document both arm pressures, each ankle reading, waveforms, the calculated ratios and the plan. Do you have questions?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: No, thank you.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello. I am a core surgical trainee. I want to assess blood flow to your legs using a Doppler and inflatable cuffs. It can feel tight for a few seconds; if it becomes painful, please tell me and we will stop. May I proceed?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Of course.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I understand your calf hurts on walking. Exactly how far, and does rest relieve it? Any pain while lying in bed, ulcers, black toes or sudden worsening?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Around 200 metres, better after a short rest; none of the others.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will examine skin, temperature, wounds and pulses first. If any limb-threatening features emerge, that changes the urgency.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: No tissue loss. Describe the set-up.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Resting and supine where possible, legs supported at heart level, appropriately sized cuffs, Doppler gel and probe; I will note any inability to lie flat as a limitation.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Both brachial systolics first, not one chosen arm; I use the higher of the two for both indices.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: They are 140 right and 150 left mmHg.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I select 150 mmHg.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: For each limb I locate dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial signals, inflate until absent and slowly deflate to identify systolic return, recording the waveform as well as pressure. Peroneal artery assessment can help where possible.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The four ankle values are left 90 and 96; right 200 and 192 mmHg. Left signal is monophasic; right arteries are difficult to compress.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Highest left 96 divided by 150 equals 0.64, suggesting peripheral arterial disease. Highest right 200 divided by 150 equals 1.33, but I would treat it cautiously.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Why cautiously when the number is higher?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: With diabetes, arterial calcification can make ankle arteries poorly compressible and inflate the result. The waveform and the clinical picture matter; a high number is not proof of normal circulation.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would organise specialist vascular review, optimise cardiovascular risk factors with the treating team, and consider toe pressures or other vascular assessment if ankle measurements are unreliable. I would not use ABPI alone to authorise compression.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: What symptoms should worry me?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: New severe pain, a cold pale foot, rapidly changing symptoms, or tissue loss warrant urgent assessment. I will give you a written plan and record all six pressure values and the waveforms.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Please summarise.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Left ABPI 0.64 with monophasic signal fits symptomatic PAD; right 1.33 may be falsely elevated with diabetes. Further clinical assessment is needed before treatment decisions.

failures.move: Dismissing newly reported rest pain/tissue loss
Declaring a high index definitively normal in diabetes
Ordering high compression solely from an unreliable ABPI

recovery.when: If you gave a number too much certainty
recovery.line: I have given that number too much certainty; I need to interpret it with the Doppler signal and diabetes history.

recovery.when: If you concluded this is routine claudication
recovery.line: I should check for tissue loss and rest pain before concluding this is routine claudication.

knowledge.fact: Supine rest, both brachial pressures, both DP/PT pressures and waveform description are recommended by NICE CG147 (section 1.2, diagnosis).
Use the highest ankle pressure in each leg divided by the highest brachial pressure.
In diabetes a normal or raised ABPI does not exclude PAD.
Medial calcification in diabetes/renal disease can make ABPI misleadingly normal; correlate waveform and clinical signs.
In a person with suspected PAD ask about symptoms and assess feet and peripheral pulses.

recall.think: Is the limb threatened, and can these ankle arteries be compressed reliably?
recall.say: “I will measure both arms and both ankle arteries, then interpret the Doppler signal.”
do: Supine • cuff and Doppler • bilateral brachial, DP and PT • calculate and document.

numbers.meaning: These examples are case values, not universal treatment cut-offs.
These examples are case values, not universal treatment cut-offs.

recall.trap: High ABPI in diabetes is not a rule-out test.
recall.finish: Explain limitations, vascular review and urgent symptom safety-net.

partner.actorBrief: Opening patient line: “My left calf aches after walking; why do I need cuffs on both legs?” No extra finding is volunteered unprompted.

reveals.trigger: Only on asking about rest pain/wounds
reveals.finding: “No wounds, no pain in bed and no sudden change.”
Left posterior tibial 90, dorsalis pedis 96; right posterior tibial 200, dorsalis pedis 192 mmHg. Left signal monophasic and right signal poorly compressible.

Pressure values are supplied by examiner only after candidate requests measurements; waveform quality is disclosed when requested or as part of result panel. Examiner uses the given values consistently.

curveballs.prompt: Cue 1 after calculation: “Does the high right number mean that leg is fine?”
curveballs.safeAnswer: Not necessarily. Diabetes can cause stiff vessels and spuriously high or normal ABPI readings, so I do not exclude disease on the right from this value alone.

curveballs.prompt: Cue 2 after management plan: “Can I start compression socks?”
curveballs.safeAnswer: Compression decisions need the full assessment, not this ratio alone.
